## Introduction

In Labs 5 and 6 we classified breast tumors from 30 measurements. Nobody can
look at a table with 30 columns and see what is in it. This lab asks two
questions about the same data:

> *Can 30 correlated measurements be squeezed into a few numbers without
> losing much? And can those few numbers still tell a benign tumor from a
> malignant one?*

The first question is **principal component analysis (PCA)**. The second is
**principal components regression (PCR)**: fit the regression on the first
few principal components instead of on the original features.

The plan:

0. **Look at the data.** Thirty features, many of them close to copies of
   each other.
1. **Scaling.** Why PCA on the raw data tells us nothing.
2. **PCA by hand.** Eigenvalues, loadings and scores, checked against `prcomp()`.
3. **How many components?** The scree plot and its rules of thumb.
4. **Reading the components.** What do the loadings say?
5. **A map of the tumors.** Two numbers per tumor, coloured by diagnosis, and
   a check on whether the biggest component is the useful one.
6. **PCA as compression.** Reconstructing the data from a few components.
7. **PCR.** Logistic regression on the first $M$ components, with $M$ chosen
   by cross-validation.

Every code cell runs live in your browser via webR, so you do not need to
install R. Packages and data load once when the page opens. Give it a few
seconds on first load. Click **Run Code** to run a cell. Run the cells in
order from the top, because later cells use objects that earlier cells make.

## A note on the tools

- **PCA has no outcome, so `caret::train()` does not apply.** We use base R's
  `prcomp()`. We also compute the eigendecomposition ourselves with `eigen()`
  and check that the two agree.
- **PCR is two steps, so we write the two steps.** The `pls` package has a
  `pcr()` function for a numeric outcome, but our outcome is a diagnosis
  (benign or malignant). So we fit the principal components, then fit a
  logistic regression on them. The slides write PCR with a linear regression,
  $Y = Z\theta + \epsilon$. For a binary outcome, the same idea gives
  $\text{logit}\, P(Y = 1) = \theta_0 + Z\theta$.

## The data: Wisconsin breast tumors

This is the same dataset as Labs 5 and 6: 569 tumors from fine-needle-aspirate
images (Street, Wolberg and Mangasarian, 1993). Ten properties of the cell
nuclei are measured (radius, texture, smoothness, and so on). For each
property the data has its mean, its standard error, and its "worst" value in
the image, giving 30 columns.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

wdbc <- read.csv("data/wdbc.csv") |>
  mutate(diagnosis = factor(diagnosis, levels = c("B", "M"),
                            labels = c("Benign", "Malignant")))

feat <- wdbc |> select(-diagnosis)   # the 30 features: all that PCA sees

dim(feat)
table(wdbc$diagnosis)
```

**The diagnosis is not given to PCA.** PCA is unsupervised. We keep the
diagnosis on the side and use it only to check what PCA found.

### Many features say the same thing

A tumor with a large radius also has a large perimeter and a large area. The
correlation matrix shows how much of this there is. The 30 columns come in
three blocks of 10 (means, standard errors, worst values), in the same order
in each block.

```{webr}
cm <- cor(feat)

ggplot(as.data.frame(as.table(cm)), aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3B4992", mid = "white", high = "#EE0000",
                       limits = c(-1, 1), name = "correlation") +
  labs(title = "Correlations between the 30 features") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, size = 8),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8),
        axis.title = element_blank())

(sum(abs(cm) > 0.9) - ncol(feat)) / 2    # pairs of features with |r| > 0.9
cor(feat$radius_mean, feat$area_mean)
```

21 pairs of features have a correlation above 0.9 in absolute value. The
radius and the area of the same tumor have a correlation of 0.987. These
columns carry much less than 30 separate pieces of information. That is
what PCA exploits: if features move together, a few combinations of them
can stand in for all of them.

# Part 1 — Scaling comes first

The slides say PCA finds the direction of maximum variance. Variance depends
on the units. Look at the variances of the features:

```{webr}
round(sort(sapply(feat, var), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3], 0)
round(sort(sapply(feat, var))[1:3], 6)
```

`area_worst` has a variance of about 324,000. Some features have a variance
below 0.0001. Areas are measured in the hundreds, smoothness in hundredths. What
does PCA do with the raw data?

```{webr}
pca_raw <- prcomp(feat)                      # scale. = FALSE: raw units

round(summary(pca_raw)$importance[2, 1:3], 3)   # share of variance, PC1 to PC3
round(sort(abs(pca_raw$rotation[, 1]), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3], 3)
```

The first component "explains" 98% of the variance. But look at its loadings:
`area_worst` has weight 0.85, `area_mean` 0.52, and nothing else matters. PC1
is just the area of the tumor. It is a fact about the units, not about the
tumors. The other 27 features have such small variances that PCA cannot see
them.

We **center and scale** every feature to mean 0 and variance 1 first. Then all
30 features have the same say, and PCA looks at the *correlations* between
them. In `prcomp()`, this is `scale. = TRUE`.

```{webr}
pca <- prcomp(feat, scale. = TRUE)

# The sign of a component is arbitrary: -phi is as good as phi. We flip PC1 so
# that a larger score means a more abnormal tumor.
pca$rotation[, 1] <- -pca$rotation[, 1]
pca$x[, 1]        <- -pca$x[, 1]

round(summary(pca)$importance[2, 1:5], 3)
```

Now PC1 explains 44% of the variance, which is a more honest number.
**Rule: scale before PCA, unless the features share a unit and you have a
reason to keep their natural scale.**

# Part 2 — PCA by hand

::: {.callout-tip}
## Do this on paper first

In class we found the loadings by maximizing variance. Here is the smallest
case where you can do it all by hand. Take **two standardized features** with
correlation $\rho$. Their correlation matrix is
$R = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

1. Find the two eigenvalues of $R$. (Solve $\det(R - \lambda I) = 0$.) What
   is their sum? Why must it equal 2?
2. Find the unit-length eigenvector for each eigenvalue. These are the
   loadings $(\phi_{11}, \phi_{21})$ and $(\phi_{12}, \phi_{22})$. Check that
   they are orthogonal and that $\phi_{1m}^2 + \phi_{2m}^2 = 1$.
3. What is the proportion of variance explained by PC1, as a function of
   $\rho$?
4. What happens when $\rho = 0$? When $\rho$ is close to 1? What would you
   conclude about PCA on features that are uncorrelated?

Then use your answer for `radius_mean` and `area_mean`, which have
$\rho = 0.987$, and compare with the code below.
:::

```{webr}
two <- feat[, c("radius_mean", "area_mean")]
rho <- cor(two)[1, 2]

c(rho = rho, PVE1_by_hand = (1 + rho) / 2)

q <- prcomp(two, scale. = TRUE)
round(summary(q)$importance[2, ], 4)      # PVE from prcomp
round(q$rotation, 3)                      # loadings from prcomp
```

The eigenvalues are $1 + \rho$ and $1 - \rho$, the loadings are
$(1, 1)/\sqrt{2}$ and $(1, -1)/\sqrt{2}$, and PC1 explains $(1 + \rho)/2$ of
the variance. PC1 is the *average* of the two standardized features (size),
and PC2 is their *difference* (what is left over). When $\rho$ is close to 1,
the average carries nearly all of the information, and one number replaces two.
When $\rho = 0$, both eigenvalues are 1: there is no direction worth keeping.

### All 30 features

The slides say PCA "can be solved via eigen decomposition". The loadings are
the eigenvectors of the correlation matrix of the data, and the variances of
the components are its eigenvalues. We check this on the full data:

```{webr}
e <- eigen(cor(feat))

# variances of the components = eigenvalues
all.equal(e$values, pca$sdev^2)

# loadings = eigenvectors (up to sign)
max(abs(abs(e$vectors) - abs(pca$rotation)))
```

Both agree. The scores are the data projected onto the loading directions,
$Z = X \Phi$, with $X$ the scaled data:

```{webr}
Z_manual <- scale(feat) %*% pca$rotation
max(abs(Z_manual - pca$x))                        # same as pca$x

round(apply(pca$x, 2, var)[1:3], 2)               # variances of PC1 to PC3
round(e$values[1:3], 2)                           # the eigenvalues
sum(e$values)                                     # total variance = p = 30
```

Two more properties from the slides can be checked here:

```{webr}
# the scores of different components are uncorrelated
cs <- cor(pca$x)
max(abs(cs[upper.tri(cs)]))

# every loading vector has length 1
round(colSums(pca$rotation[, 1:3]^2), 3)
```

The correlations are zero to machine precision (the number printed is of the
order $10^{-14}$). That is the "uncorrelated with the previous components"
constraint, and it is why PCR will not suffer from collinearity in Part 7.

# Part 3 — How many components?

The proportion of variance explained (PVE) by component $m$ is
$\lambda_m / \sum_j \lambda_j$. Here the denominator is 30. The **scree plot**
shows the PVE for each component, and the cumulative PVE shows what is kept.

```{webr}
pve  <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
cpve <- cumsum(pve)

p_scree <- ggplot(data.frame(PC = 1:30, pve), aes(PC, pve)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(y = "proportion of variance explained", title = "Scree plot") +
  theme_bw()
p_cum <- ggplot(data.frame(PC = 1:30, cpve), aes(PC, cpve)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.8, 0.9, 0.95), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#EE0000") +
  labs(y = "cumulative PVE", title = "Cumulative PVE") +
  theme_bw()

grid.arrange(p_scree, p_cum, nrow = 1)

round(rbind(PVE = pve, cumulative = cpve)[, 1:10], 3)
```

Three rules of thumb, and they do not agree:

```{webr}
sapply(c("80%" = 0.80, "90%" = 0.90, "95%" = 0.95),
       function(t) which(cpve >= t)[1])    # smallest M reaching each threshold
sum(pca$sdev^2 > 1)                        # components with variance above 1
```

- **Elbow.** The scree plot bends around component 3 or 4. After that, each
  component adds little.
- **Cumulative PVE.** 5 components keep 80% of the variance, 7 keep 90%, and
  10 keep 95%. The slides suggest the smallest $M$ that reaches 80%.
- **Variance above 1.** A component with variance below 1 explains less than
  one original standardized feature. Six components pass this test.

So the 30 features can be summarized by roughly 5 to 10 numbers. There is no
single right answer, because without an outcome there is nothing to
cross-validate. When there *is* an outcome, as in PCR (Part 7), we can choose
$M$ by cross-validation.

# Part 4 — Reading the components

A component is a recipe: a weight (loading) for each of the 30 standardized
features. The three biggest:

```{webr}
load3 <- data.frame(round(pca$rotation[, 1:3], 2))
load3$feature <- factor(rownames(load3), levels = rev(rownames(load3)))

load3 |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(PC1:PC3, names_to = "PC", values_to = "loading") |>
  ggplot(aes(PC, feature, fill = loading)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", loading)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3B4992", mid = "white", high = "#EE0000",
                       limits = c(-0.5, 0.5), name = "loading") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

- **PC1: overall abnormality.** All 30 loadings have the same sign (after our
  flip, positive). A tumor with a high PC1 score is high on nearly every
  feature. The biggest weights are on concavity, concave points, compactness
  and the size features (perimeter, radius). The smallest are on texture and
  smoothness. PC1 is a weighted average that mostly measures the size and
  irregularity of the nuclei.
- **PC2: size against roughness.** The size features (radius, area, perimeter)
  have positive loadings. The fractal dimension features (a measure of how
  rough the outline is) have the largest negative ones. A high PC2 means large
  nuclei with a smooth outline. A low PC2 means smaller nuclei with a rough
  outline. A contrast like this is a pattern in the data that no single
  feature shows.
- **PC3: variability within the image.** The largest loadings are on the
  *standard-error* features (`texture_se`, `smoothness_se`, `symmetry_se`).
  This component is about how much the nuclei within one image vary, not
  about their typical values.

**A warning.** Names like "abnormality" or "roughness" are our reading of the
loadings. PCA does not know what the features mean. Another analyst can
name the same component differently, and a component can mix several things.

# Part 5 — A map of the tumors

Two numbers per tumor can be drawn. We plot the first two scores and colour
by diagnosis. PCA never saw the diagnosis.

```{webr}
scores <- data.frame(pca$x[, 1:3], diagnosis = wdbc$diagnosis)

ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = diagnosis)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(title = "30 measurements, 2 numbers per tumor") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

tapply(scores$PC1, scores$diagnosis, mean)
mean((scores$PC1 > 0) == (scores$diagnosis == "Malignant"))   # PC1 > 0 means malignant
```

The two diagnoses fall in different parts of the plot, mostly along PC1. A
single rule, "PC1 above 0 means malignant", is right for 92% of the tumors,
with no labels used to build it. This is what the slides mean by "a simple
visualization that shows a clear underlying pattern". It also tells us that a
predictive model has a good chance.

### Is the biggest component the useful one?

PCA orders components by *variance*. It does not know the diagnosis, so there
is no promise that the highest-variance direction is the one that separates
the groups. Here we can check. For each component, the AUC of its score for
telling malignant from benign (0.5 is no signal, 1 is perfect; we take
`max(auc, 1 - auc)` because the sign is arbitrary):

```{webr}
auc <- function(s, y) {                 # rank-based AUC; y is TRUE for malignant
  r <- rank(s)
  (sum(r[y]) - sum(y) * (sum(y) + 1) / 2) / (sum(y) * sum(!y))
}

auc_pc <- sapply(1:10, function(j) auc(pca$x[, j], wdbc$diagnosis == "Malignant"))

round(setNames(pmax(auc_pc, 1 - auc_pc), paste0("PC", 1:10)), 3)
```

PC1 has an AUC of 0.97. Every other component is at 0.62 or below. In these
data, the direction of most variance is also the direction that separates the
groups. That is good luck, and it is what makes PCR work in Part 7. In other
data, the signal can sit in a component with little variance. Then PCR with a
small $M$ throws it away.

# Part 6 — PCA as compression

The slides gave PCA a second description: the $M$ components give the best
$M$-dimensional approximation of the data. We build that approximation from
the first $M$ scores and loadings, $\hat X = Z_{1:M}\, \Phi_{1:M}^\top$, and
measure what is lost:

```{webr}
Xs <- scale(feat)

recon_err <- function(M) {
  Xhat <- pca$x[, 1:M, drop = FALSE] %*% t(pca$rotation[, 1:M, drop = FALSE])
  sum((Xs - Xhat)^2) / sum(Xs^2)       # share of the variation lost
}

Ms <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 30)
round(rbind(M = Ms,
            lost_in_reconstruction = sapply(Ms, recon_err),
            one_minus_cumulative_PVE = 1 - cpve[Ms]), 3)
```

The two rows are the same. The share lost when we rebuild the data from $M$
components is exactly $1 -$ the cumulative PVE. So "keep the directions of
maximum variance" and "make the reconstruction error as small as possible"
are the same goal. With 10 components, we keep 95% of the information in
the data, and we use a third of the columns.

# Part 7 — Principal components regression

Now the outcome. We want to predict the diagnosis from the 30 features.

### Why not use all 30?

As in Lab 6, we use the same split: 75% of the tumors for training, and 25% for
testing.

```{webr}
library(caret)

set.seed(2155)
idx   <- createDataPartition(wdbc$diagnosis, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
train <- wdbc[idx, ]
test  <- wdbc[-idx, ]

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))

full_glm <- glm(diagnosis ~ ., data = train, family = binomial)
summary(abs(coef(full_glm)))
```

R warns that the algorithm did not converge. The features are so correlated,
and the classes so separable in 30 dimensions, that the coefficients grow
without limit. The estimates have no meaning. This is the instability of OLS
under collinearity that the slides described. Lab 6 fixed it with a penalty
(the lasso). PCR fixes it by changing the predictors.

### Step 1: PCA on the training set only

PCA uses only the features, not the outcome. Even so, we fit it on the
**training** tumors, and then we **project** the test tumors with the training
means, SDs and loadings. We do not refit on the test set: a new patient arrives
one at a time, and our model must be able to score each of them alone.

```{webr}
pca_tr <- prcomp(train[, -1], scale. = TRUE)

Z_train <- pca_tr$x                                   # 427 x 30 scores
Z_test  <- predict(pca_tr, test[, -1])                # 142 x 30 scores
y_train <- as.integer(train$diagnosis == "Malignant")
y_test  <- as.integer(test$diagnosis == "Malignant")

dim(Z_train); dim(Z_test)
```

### Step 2: Choose $M$ by cross-validation

For each $M$ from 1 to 20, we fit a logistic regression on the first $M$
scores. We use 10-fold cross-validation and measure two things: the **deviance**
(a measure of fit that punishes confident mistakes, lower is better) and the
**accuracy**.

To keep the code short, PCA is fitted once on the training set, and then the
folds are used for the regression only. PCA never sees $y$, so the leak is
small.

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
set.seed(1)
folds <- createFolds(train$diagnosis, k = 10)

cv_pcr <- function(M) {
  d <- as.data.frame(Z_train[, 1:M, drop = FALSE])
  res <- sapply(folds, function(f) {
    fit <- suppressWarnings(glm(y_train[-f] ~ ., data = d[-f, , drop = FALSE],
                                family = binomial))
    ph  <- predict(fit, d[f, , drop = FALSE], type = "response")
    ph  <- pmin(pmax(ph, 1e-12), 1 - 1e-12)
    c(accuracy = mean((ph > 0.5) == y_train[f]),
      deviance = -2 * mean(y_train[f] * log(ph) + (1 - y_train[f]) * log(1 - ph)))
  })
  rowMeans(res)
}

Mgrid <- 1:20
cv <- data.frame(M = Mgrid, t(sapply(Mgrid, cv_pcr)))
best_M <- cv$M[which.min(cv$deviance)]
best_M
```

```{webr}
p_dev <- ggplot(cv, aes(M, deviance)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_M, colour = "#EE0000", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "number of components M", y = "CV deviance (log scale)",
       title = "CV deviance: lower is better") +
  theme_bw()
p_acc <- ggplot(cv, aes(M, accuracy)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_M, colour = "#EE0000", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "number of components M", y = "CV accuracy",
       title = "CV accuracy: higher is better") +
  theme_bw()

grid.arrange(p_dev, p_acc, nrow = 1)
round(cv[c(1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14, 16, 20), ], 3)
```

The deviance has a clear U shape. It falls fast up to about 4 components,
reaches its lowest value at $M = 8$ (the red line), and then rises. Past about
15 components it explodes, because the model has started to separate the
training data perfectly (the same problem as the 30-feature fit above). The
accuracy is flat, about 97%, from 4 to 14 components. So the choice of $M$
does not need to be exact: anything in that range works. Compare this with
the rules of thumb in Part 3 (5 to 10 components). Here the outcome gives a
sharper reason to stop than the variance alone.

### Step 3: Fit and test

```{webr}
fit_pcr <- function(M) {
  d <- as.data.frame(Z_train[, 1:M, drop = FALSE])
  suppressWarnings(glm(y_train ~ ., data = d, family = binomial))
}

test_acc <- function(M) {
  ph <- predict(fit_pcr(M), as.data.frame(Z_test[, 1:M, drop = FALSE]),
                type = "response")
  mean((ph > 0.5) == y_test)
}

pcr_best <- fit_pcr(best_M)
ph_test  <- predict(pcr_best, as.data.frame(Z_test[, 1:best_M]), type = "response")

table(truth = test$diagnosis,
      predicted = factor(ph_test > 0.5, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("Benign", "Malignant")))
round(sapply(c("M=1" = 1, "M=2" = 2, "M=5" = 5, "M=8" = 8, "M=15" = 15, "M=30" = 30),
             test_acc), 3)
```

The model with $M = 8$ components classifies about 98% of the held-out tumors
correctly (3 mistakes in 142). The model with all 30 components (which uses the same information
as the 30-feature logistic regression) does worse, at about 94%. The test set has
only 142 tumors, so one tumor is 0.7 percentage points. Do not read much into
differences of one or two tumors between neighbouring values of $M$. The
cross-validation curve, which uses all 427 training tumors, is more reliable.

### Back to the original features

The price of PCR is interpretability: the coefficients $\theta_m$ belong to
components. But the model is still linear in the features. Since
$Z_m = \sum_j \phi_{jm} X_j$, the coefficient on the original (standardized)
feature $j$ is
$$\beta_j = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \theta_m \, \phi_{jm}.$$
The slides call this *constraining* the coefficients: the 30 values of
$\beta_j$ are not free, because they are built from only $M$ numbers.

```{webr}
theta <- coef(pcr_best)                              # intercept + M coefficients
beta  <- pca_tr$rotation[, 1:best_M] %*% theta[-1]   # one beta per feature

# check: the same linear predictor, computed from the features directly
X_test_std <- scale(test[, -1], center = pca_tr$center, scale = pca_tr$scale)
lp_features <- theta[1] + X_test_std %*% beta
lp_scores   <- predict(pcr_best, as.data.frame(Z_test[, 1:best_M]))
max(abs(lp_features - lp_scores))

b <- data.frame(feature = rownames(beta), beta = beta[, 1])
b <- b[order(-abs(b$beta)), ][1:10, ]

ggplot(b, aes(beta, reorder(feature, abs(beta)), fill = beta > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#EE0000", "FALSE" = "#3B4992")) +
  labs(x = "coefficient on the standardized feature", y = NULL,
       title = "PCR: the ten largest coefficients") +
  theme_bw()
```

The two ways of computing the linear predictor agree. Notice that the weight
is spread over groups of related features (several size features, several
concavity features), because the components give related features similar
loadings. The lasso in Lab 6 behaves differently: it tends to keep one
feature from each correlated group and drop the rest. Neither is "right".
PCR is a good choice when you want to use all the information in a group of
correlated measurements. The lasso is a good choice when you want a short
list of features to measure.

**Two cautions about PCR.**

- It chooses the components *without looking at the outcome*. It worked here
  because PC1 separates the classes (Part 5). If the signal were in a
  low-variance component, PCR with a small $M$ would miss it.
- It is not a feature-selection method. Every component uses all 30 features,
  so you still need to measure all 30 to score a new patient.

## Try it yourself

**1. The two-feature formula.** For `compactness_mean` and `concavity_mean`,
compute $\rho$, the PVE of PC1 from $(1 + \rho)/2$, and check it against
`prcomp()`. Are these two features as redundant as radius and area?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_two_features
two2 <- feat[, c("compactness_mean", "concavity_mean")]
rho2 <- cor(two2)[1, 2]
c(rho = rho2, PVE1_by_hand = (1 + ______) / 2)
round(summary(prcomp(two2, scale. = TRUE))$importance[2, 1], 4)
```

**2. How many components for 95%?** Find the smallest $M$ whose cumulative
PVE is at least 95%, then compute the share of variance lost in the
reconstruction with that $M$ (use `recon_err()` from Part 6). Does it match?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_95
M95 <- which(cpve >= ______)[1]
M95
recon_err(M95)
```

**3. Skip the first component.** PCR uses the *first* $M$ components. What if
we use two components, but not PC1? Fit the logistic regression on `Z_train`
columns 2 and 3, and compute its test accuracy. Compare it with $M = 2$ from
Part 7. What does this tell you about *why* PCR works on these data?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_skip_pc1
d_23 <- as.data.frame(Z_train[, c(2, ______)])
fit_23 <- suppressWarnings(glm(y_train ~ ., data = d_23, family = binomial))
ph_23 <- predict(fit_23, as.data.frame(Z_test[, c(2, 3)]), type = "response")
mean((ph_23 > 0.5) == y_test)
```

**4. Forget to scale.** Fit PCA on the training features with
`scale. = FALSE`, and repeat the cross-validation with `Z_train` replaced by
the unscaled scores. (Copy `cv_pcr()`, and change the first line inside it.)
Which $M$ does cross-validation choose now? Is the best CV accuracy as high as
before? Is the test accuracy at that $M$ much different? Compare how badly
scaling hurt the *description* (Part 1: PC1 was just the area) with how much
it hurts the *prediction*. Why can the later components make up for a poor PC1?

**5. A different split.** Change the seed in `set.seed(2155)` and rerun Part 7.
How much does the best $M$ move? How much does the test accuracy move?

## Things worth remembering

- **PCA finds new axes that capture variance.** Each component is a weighted
  sum of the features. The first has the most variance, and each later one has
  the most variance among those uncorrelated with the earlier ones.
- **Scale first.** PCA follows variance, and variance depends on units. On raw
  data, one feature with a big unit took over the first component.
- **PCA is an eigendecomposition.** The loadings are eigenvectors of the
  correlation matrix, and the variances of the scores are its eigenvalues.
  With two standardized features, PC1 explains $(1 + \rho)/2$.
- **There is no single right $M$ in PCA.** The elbow, 80% cumulative PVE and
  variance above 1 gave 3 to 4, 5, and 6 components. Use the rule to get a
  range, not an answer.
- **Variance and compression are one idea.** The error of rebuilding the data
  from $M$ components is $1 -$ the cumulative PVE.
- **PCR is regression on the first $M$ scores.** The scores are uncorrelated,
  so the instability from correlated features goes away. $M$ is chosen by
  cross-validation. The coefficients can be mapped back to the features by
  $\beta_j = \sum_m \theta_m \phi_{jm}$.
- **PCR does not see the outcome when it builds the components.** It works
  when the high-variance directions are the useful ones. Check this before
  you trust it.
- **Components are not features you can measure on their own.** A PCR model
  still needs all $p$ original measurements for each new patient, and the
  names we give to components are our reading, not something in the data.
